concepts.title: Confirmation Bias
concepts.tagline: Your mind is not a truth-seeking machine — it is a belief-defending machine.
keyPoints: Once you hold a belief, your mind automatically recruits evidence for it, dismisses evidence against it, and interprets ambiguous information in its favour — all without you noticing.
It operates at three stages: what you seek, how you interpret, and what you remember. Confirming evidence sticks; disconfirming evidence fades.
The most dangerous form: the feeling of certainty. The more certain you feel, the more likely you are running on unexamined assumption, not verified truth.
The antidote is not willpower — it is structure. Ask 'What would prove me wrong?' before committing to any conclusion.
strategicSteps: Before making any decision, spend 5 minutes actively arguing the opposite position as strongly as you can.
Ask one question daily: 'What evidence have I been ignoring or dismissing this week?'
When you feel very certain about something, treat that certainty as a signal to slow down — not to speed up.
Keep a prediction journal: write down your expectations before events, then review after. Your miss-rate will surprise you.

business.title: The Hiring Trap
business.situation: You interview a candidate who reminds you of your best employee. Within 10 minutes you've decided you want to hire them. The rest of the interview becomes a formality.
business.whatHappens: Every answer they give, you interpret generously. Red flags get rationalised. Questions become confirmatory ('I'm sure you're good at X, right?') rather than probing. You hire someone who looks right but isn't right.
applicationSteps: Before the interview, write down 3 specific things that would make you NOT hire this person. Actively look for those.
Assign one interviewer the explicit role of 'devil's advocate' — their job is to find problems, not potential.
After the interview, before discussing, everyone writes their assessment independently. Sharing first creates anchoring bias.
Ask: 'What is the strongest argument against hiring this person?' If you can't answer it, you haven't thought hard enough.

social.title: The First Impression Lock
social.situation: You meet someone at a party and within minutes form an impression — warm, cold, trustworthy, shifty. For the rest of the evening, everything they do confirms what you already decided.
social.whatHappens: Ambiguous behaviour gets filtered through the lens of your first impression. A quiet moment = 'see, they're standoffish.' An enthusiastic comment = 'see, they're trying too hard.' The impression becomes self-sealing.
applicationSteps: Notice the moment you form a first impression. That's the moment confirmation bias begins.
Deliberately look for one piece of evidence that contradicts your impression before the conversation ends.
Ask yourself: 'What would this person's best friend say about them?' This forces a more charitable interpretation.
Before writing someone off socially, ask: 'Have I given them a genuine chance, or have I been collecting evidence for a verdict I already reached?'

intimate.title: The Recurring Argument
intimate.situation: You and your partner have a recurring conflict. You're convinced you're right. Every new incident becomes more proof. They feel the same way about their position. The argument never resolves.
intimate.whatHappens: Both of you are running confirmation bias at full power. You remember every time they did the thing that bothers you; they remember every time you did theirs. You've each built a case file. Neither case file is false — it's just incomplete.
applicationSteps: Before the next difficult conversation, write down the 3 strongest points in their favour — not yours. Read them out loud to yourself first.
Ask: 'When was the last time I updated my view of this person based on something they did well?' If you can't remember, your mental model of them is frozen in a negative moment.
In the conversation: 'I want to understand what I'm doing that contributes to this' — before any accusation. This breaks the confirmation loop.
Agree on a 'pause word' when either of you feels the argument becoming circular. Use it. Step away for 20 minutes before returning.

concepts.title: The Stoic Dichotomy of Control
concepts.tagline: Some things are up to us. Everything else is not. This distinction changes everything.
keyPoints: Epictetus divided all of existence into two categories: 'up to us' (your judgments, impulses, desires, and responses) and 'not up to us' (your body, reputation, outcomes, other people's actions).
Most suffering comes from treating 'not up to us' things as though they were 'up to us' — investing energy in what you cannot control, and neglecting what you can.
This is not passivity. It is strategic focus. You act fully and excellently on what is within your domain; you release what is not.
Marcus Aurelius tested every morning challenge against this dichotomy: 'Is this up to me or not?' The answer determined where he put his energy.
strategicSteps: Each morning, write one current worry or challenge. Then write two columns: 'What I can control' and 'What I cannot.' Put your energy entirely in column one.
When something goes wrong, ask before reacting: 'Is my distress about what happened, or about what I think it means?' The first is often unavoidable. The second is always a choice.
Practice 'preferred indifference': pursue goals with full effort, but do not attach your peace to the outcome. The effort is yours; the result is not.
Weekly: identify one thing you've been trying to control that you genuinely cannot. Write a conscious decision to release it.

business.title: The Outcome You Can't Control
business.situation: You've prepared a pitch for months. The client meeting goes brilliantly. Then they go silent for two weeks. You refresh your email constantly. Your mood tracks their response time.
business.whatHappens: Your energy is entirely in 'not up to us' territory. The client's decision, their timeline, their internal politics — none of it is yours to control. Meanwhile, the worry is consuming mental bandwidth that could go toward the next pitch.
applicationSteps: After any pitch or proposal, immediately write: 'What is in my control now?' (follow-up quality, timing, other opportunities). Put your energy there.
Set one scheduled 'check-in' time per day for outstanding proposals. Outside that window, close the tab. The refreshing is not action — it is anxiety disguised as action.
Prepare a 'release statement': 'I did the best preparation I could. The outcome is now outside my domain.' Say it aloud after sending any important proposal.
Ask: 'If this doesn't come through, what will I do next?' Having the answer removes the catastrophising that makes waiting so painful.

social.title: What They Think of You
social.situation: You said something at a dinner party that landed badly. On the way home, you replay it. For the next three days, you wonder what everyone thought. You consider sending a message to clarify, then reconsider, then reconsider again.
social.whatHappens: You're treating other people's opinions as if they were within your control. They aren't. What you can control: whether you apologise if genuinely needed, and how you behave next time.
applicationSteps: Ask: 'Is there something I can genuinely do to address this?' If yes, do it once, clearly. If no, the rumination is a 'not up to us' problem wearing 'up to us' clothes.
Write down what actually happened, not what you imagine people thought. The gap between those two things is where most social anxiety lives.
Practice the Stoic 'view from above': imagine watching the scene from 1000 feet up. How significant does it look from there?
Ask: 'Am I ruminating because I actually did something wrong, or because I care what they think?' The first deserves action. The second deserves release.

intimate.title: Trying to Change Your Partner
intimate.situation: Your partner has a habit that bothers you. You've mentioned it. Then mentioned it again. More directly. It hasn't changed. Now it's a source of persistent tension between you.
intimate.whatHappens: You're in 'not up to us' territory. Your partner's behaviour is not yours to control. What IS yours: how you respond to it, whether you continue to bring it up, how you communicate your needs, and whether this is a dealbreaker.
applicationSteps: Write two columns: 'What I have control over in this relationship' and 'What I do not.' Read the second column and genuinely ask: 'Am I making my peace contingent on things that aren't mine to control?'
Shift from trying to change behaviour to expressing a need: 'When X happens, I feel Y. What I need is Z.' This is in your domain — their response is not.
Ask yourself: 'If this never changed, could I be at peace with this relationship?' This is the honest question. The answer guides the decision.
Practice 'amor fati' in small things: when something they do bothers you, try — even once — choosing to find it acceptable rather than fighting it. Notice what that feels like.

concepts.title: Cognitive Biases
concepts.tagline: Your brain runs on shortcuts that were brilliant for survival and are quietly sabotaging your modern decisions.
keyPoints: The mind has two systems (Kahneman). System 1 is fast, automatic, emotional — it generates instant impressions and is the source of almost every bias. System 2 is slow, effortful, logical — but it's lazy and usually just rubber-stamps whatever System 1 already decided. Biases happen when System 2 fails to check System 1's work.

Biases are not stupidity or carelessness. They are efficient heuristics — mental shortcuts that were adaptive in ancestral environments (snap threat-detection, fast social judgement) but misfire in a world of statistics, markets, and strangers. Intelligent people are NOT more protected; they're often better at constructing clever justifications for biased conclusions.

The most consequential biases cluster in predictable places: how we judge other people (fundamental attribution error, halo effect), how we handle gains and losses (loss aversion, sunk cost), how we estimate likelihood (availability, representativeness), and how we defend what we already believe (confirmation bias, anchoring).

You cannot eliminate biases by knowing about them — System 1 operates below conscious control. Awareness alone barely helps. What works is STRUCTURE: checklists, outside views, deliberate friction, and decision rules that don't depend on in-the-moment judgement.

The bias blind spot: we readily see bias in others and feel ourselves to be the rational exception. This meta-bias is why 'just be objective' never works — your sense of being objective is itself produced by System 1.
strategicSteps: Build decision friction for anything important. Before a consequential choice, force a 24-hour gap and write down your reasoning. This recruits System 2 into a decision System 1 wants to make instantly.

Use the 'outside view'. Instead of asking 'how will MY project go?' (optimism bias guaranteed), ask 'how do projects like this usually go?' Base rates beat gut feeling. Kahneman calls this the single most useful debiasing move.

Run a pre-mortem. Before committing, imagine it's a year later and the decision failed catastrophically. Write the story of how. This surfaces the risks confirmation bias and optimism bias hid from you.

Separate the person from the situation. When judging someone's behaviour, deliberately ask 'what situation could make a reasonable person act this way?' before concluding it's their character. This directly counters the fundamental attribution error.
Make the bias work FOR you. Loss aversion (losses hurt ~2x more than gains feel good) is a tool: stake money you'll lose if you skip the gym; the pain of loss out-motivates the pull of comfort.

business.title: The Sunk-Cost Project That Won't Die
business.situation: Your team has spent 18 months and a large budget on a product feature. The data now clearly shows customers don't want it. Yet every meeting ends with 'we've come too far to stop now — let's push through.' More money goes in.
business.whatHappens: This is the sunk cost fallacy compounded by loss aversion and confirmation bias. The money already spent is gone regardless — it should be irrelevant to the forward decision. But abandoning the project feels like 'losing' the investment, so the team keeps throwing good resources after bad, and selectively highlights any data scrap that suggests it might still work.
applicationSteps: Reframe the question to erase the past: 'Knowing only what we know today, with this budget, would we START this project right now?' If no, the sunk cost is talking.
Make the loss explicit and bounded: 'We will lose the 18 months either way. The only real choice is whether we also lose the next 6.'
Assign someone to build the strongest case for KILLING it. Without a designated challenger, confirmation bias guarantees only pro-continuation evidence gets aired.
Set a kill-criterion in advance for the NEXT project: 'If by month 3 metric X isn't above Y, we stop — decided now, while we're unbiased.'

social.title: The Halo Effect in a New Acquaintance
social.situation: You meet someone polished, articulate, and confident at a networking event. You immediately assume they're also competent, trustworthy, and successful — and you start agreeing with their opinions more readily than you would with anyone else.
social.whatHappens: The halo effect: one salient positive trait (charisma) bleeds into unrelated judgements (competence, honesty). It's how confident frauds succeed and quiet experts get overlooked. Your System 1 built an entire character profile from a 30-second impression, and confirmation bias will now defend it.
applicationSteps: Separate the traits you've actually observed from the ones you're inferring. 'I've seen they're articulate. I have zero evidence yet about whether they're competent or honest.'
Look specifically for disconfirming evidence — the thing the halo is hiding. Charismatic people get fewer hard questions; ask one.
Delay consequential trust. Charisma is real-time; reliability only shows over repeated interactions. Let time, not first impression, calibrate your judgement.
Invert it for the overlooked: when someone is awkward or unpolished, deliberately ask 'what might this person be excellent at that their delivery is hiding?'

intimate.title: The Fundamental Attribution Error in Conflict
intimate.situation: Your partner forgets something important to you. Your instant interpretation: 'They don't care. They're inconsiderate.' But last week when YOU forgot something, you explained it as 'I was overwhelmed and exhausted' — a situation, not a flaw.
intimate.whatHappens: The fundamental attribution error: we explain others' behaviour by their character ('they're selfish') and our own identical behaviour by circumstances ('I was busy'). This asymmetry is the engine of most relationship conflict — each person experiences themselves as reasonable and the other as flawed.
applicationSteps: Catch the character verdict as it forms ('they ARE inconsiderate') and convert it into a situational question ('what was going on for them today?').
Apply the symmetry test: 'When I did this exact thing, what was my explanation? Would that same explanation be available to them?' Usually it is.
Lead with the situation, not the accusation: 'Hey, you forgot X — was something going on?' opens a door; 'You never think about me' slams it.
Build a shared rule for the relationship: 'We assume good intent and ask about circumstances before assigning blame.' Name it in a calm moment so you can both invoke it in a heated one.

concepts.title: Logotherapy
concepts.tagline: The primary human drive isn't pleasure or power — it's meaning. And meaning can be found even in suffering you cannot escape.
keyPoints: Frankl developed logotherapy partly in Nazi concentration camps, where he observed who survived and who gave up. His conclusion: those who had a 'why' — a person to return to, a book to finish, a task only they could do — endured 'almost any how.' Meaning, not comfort, was the difference between collapse and survival.

Meaning is found in three ways, not invented from thin air: (1) through WORK or creating something — a contribution, a deed; (2) through LOVE or encountering someone — connection, beauty, experience; (3) through the ATTITUDE we take toward unavoidable suffering. The third is the radical one: when you can't change a situation, you can still choose your stance toward it, and that choice itself creates meaning.

The 'existential vacuum' is Frankl's diagnosis of modern malaise — a feeling of emptiness, boredom, and 'what's the point?' that appears when survival is handled but meaning is absent. He argued much depression, addiction, and aggression grows in this vacuum. Affluence doesn't fill it; only meaning does.

Self-transcendence is the mechanism: the more you aim directly AT happiness or meaning, the more they elude you. They arrive as by-products of devoting yourself to something — or someone — beyond yourself. 'Don't aim at success. The more you aim at it and make it a target, the more you are going to miss it.'

'Tragic optimism' is saying yes to life despite the 'tragic triad' — pain, guilt, and death. Not toxic positivity that denies suffering, but a hard-won capacity to find meaning within it. This is the opposite of both despair and forced cheerfulness.
strategicSteps: Ask the reframed question. Frankl said the question is never 'what do I want from life?' but 'what is life asking of ME, right now, in this specific situation?' Apply it to whatever you're facing today — it shifts you from passive consumer to responsible agent.

Locate your three sources weekly. Write one answer each for: what did I CREATE or contribute? Who did I genuinely CONNECT with? What unavoidable difficulty did I face, and what STANCE did I take? Gaps reveal where meaning is thin.

Practise 'dereflection' for anxiety. When you're trapped overthinking yourself (your performance, your happiness, your symptoms), deliberately redirect attention OUTWARD toward a task or person. Meaning lives outside the self, not in self-monitoring.
Find the 'why' before the 'how'. Before a hard goal or grim period, get specific about what it's FOR — who benefits, what it enables, who you become. A concrete why makes a brutal how survivable.

Reframe unavoidable suffering as a question of stance. When something genuinely cannot be changed, ask: 'Given that this is happening, what would it mean to meet it well? What is the most meaningful way to carry this?'

business.title: The Hollow Success
business.situation: You're good at your job and well paid. But Friday evenings you feel empty. The work doesn't feel like it matters. You can't tell whether you should quit, or whether the emptiness would follow you anywhere.
business.whatHappens: This is the existential vacuum in a professional skin. Competence and salary handle survival but don't supply meaning. Frankl's three sources let you diagnose precisely what's missing: most 'meaningless' jobs actually contain meaning that's gone unnoticed — or reveal a genuine misalignment worth acting on.
applicationSteps: Trace the contribution: 'Who specifically is better off because I did my work well this week?' Make it a real person, not an abstraction. Meaning hides in specifics — the colleague you unblocked, the customer you served.
Test the three sources against the job: Is there room to CREATE? To CONNECT with people you value? If both are genuinely absent and unfixable, that's real data — not a character flaw in you.
Before quitting, try changing your stance for two weeks: approach the same tasks asking 'what would doing this meaningfully look like?' Sometimes the job isn't the problem; the autopilot is.

If the vacuum persists after honest effort, ask the Frankl question: 'What is life asking of me now?' The answer might be a new role — or a meaningful pursuit OUTSIDE work that the job exists to fund.

social.title: Supporting a Friend Through the Unfixable
social.situation: A friend is facing something genuinely terrible and irreversible — a terminal diagnosis, a devastating loss. You desperately want to help but every comforting phrase ('it'll be okay', 'everything happens for a reason') feels hollow, and you can see it landing badly.
social.whatHappens: Most of us instinctively try to REMOVE suffering — minimise it, explain it, or fix it. But this suffering can't be removed, so those moves fail and can even wound. Frankl's insight: when you can't change the situation, the gift you can offer is helping someone find meaning WITHIN it, and simply not abandoning them in it.
applicationSteps: Stop trying to fix or reframe their pain. Sit in it with them. 'This is genuinely terrible, and I'm here' is worth more than any silver lining.
Don't supply meaning — that's theirs to find. Instead ask gently: 'What matters most to you in how you face this?' or 'Who or what is helping you hold on?'
Honour the dignity of their stance. Frankl saw that HOW a person bears unavoidable suffering can be a profound achievement. Name it when you see it: 'The way you're carrying this is remarkable.'
Be the concrete 'why'. Often a person's reason to keep going is the people who need them. Your steady presence can itself be part of their meaning — show up reliably, not just dramatically.

intimate.title: The Relationship That's Become Hard
intimate.situation: You're in a persistently difficult stretch with your partner — not explosive, just heavy and depleting. You keep asking 'is this still making me happy?' and the honest answer some days is no. You're wondering whether to hold on or let go.
intimate.whatHappens: Frankl would gently challenge the question itself. 'What do I want FROM this relationship?' frames you as a consumer of happiness. 'What is this relationship asking of me — and what meaning could I create in it?' frames you as a participant. The shift from extracting to contributing often reveals whether there's life left to build, or whether it's genuinely run its course.
applicationSteps: Switch the question for one week: instead of 'am I happy?', ask 'what does showing up well in this relationship ask of me right now?' Notice what that surfaces.
Find what you're avoiding. Meaning in relationships usually hides behind the conversation you're not having, the apology you're withholding, the change you're resisting. Name it.

Apply self-transcendence: stop aiming at 'being happy together' directly. Aim instead at a shared project, caring well for each other, or a difficulty you face as a team — happiness tends to return as a by-product.

Use the regret test for clarity: 'If this ended, what would I regret not having genuinely tried?' Try exactly that — fully, for a defined period. Then you'll have an answer earned through commitment, not guesswork.

concepts.title: First Principles Thinking
concepts.tagline: Strip away assumption and inherited convention until you reach what's actually true — then reason up from there.
keyPoints: Most thinking is reasoning by analogy — copying what's been done, what others do, what convention says. It's fast and socially safe, but it inherits every hidden assumption baked into the original.
First principles thinking reasons up from bedrock truths that cannot be reduced further. The formula (李善友): first principle + deduction = a rational system.

The hidden enemy is the 'continuity assumption' — the unexamined belief that the future resembles the past and here resembles elsewhere. It's smuggled into almost every conclusion and is invisible because it's foundational.
Most 'constraints' are inherited conventions, not physical laws. When something seems impossible, ask whether it's a genuine constraint or just an assumption nobody has questioned.
The most personal application: which of your beliefs, values, and identity claims are genuinely yours (reasoned and tested) versus inherited (absorbed from family, culture, peers) and never examined?
strategicSteps: Pick one assumption you treat as fact and ask 'is this actually true, or just a continuity assumption?'
For any belief, keep asking 'why is this true?' until you reach a direct observation or a logical necessity — or discover you've hit unexamined convention.
Decompose 'impossible' goals into components and ask which parts are genuinely fixed vs. merely conventional.
Ask of any important belief: 'If I'd been raised in a different family or culture, would I still hold this?'
Notice what your community treats as obvious — that's where the unexamined axioms (and the opportunities) hide.

business.title: The Cost Everyone Accepts
business.situation: Your industry 'knows' a certain cost is fixed — 'that's just what it costs.' Everyone plans around it. Margins stay thin because nobody questions the number.
business.whatHappens: Reasoning by analogy ('this is what it has always cost') hides that the cost is a convention, not a physical law. Musk's battery example: $600/kWh was convention; the raw materials cost ~$80. The gap was unexamined assumption.
applicationSteps: Ask 'what is this actually made of, at its most basic, and what does THAT cost?'
Separate genuine constraints (physics, math) from inherited conventions (how it's been done).
Rebuild the solution from the verified bedrock, not from competitors' approaches.
Test the riskiest assumption cheaply before committing.

social.title: The 'Should' You Never Chose
social.situation: You feel obligated to do something socially — a tradition, an expectation, a way of doing things — that you've never actually questioned. It just feels like what one does.
social.whatHappens: The 'should' is a continuity assumption inherited from your environment. It feels like a law of reality, but it's a convention you absorbed and never examined.
applicationSteps: Ask: 'Where did this rule come from? Did I choose it or absorb it?'
Ask: 'Would someone from a very different background find this obviously necessary, or ask why?'
Keep what survives examination; consciously drop what doesn't.
Decide on purpose, rather than by inherited default.

intimate.title: The Inherited Relationship Script
intimate.situation: You and your partner keep running a script about how relationships 'should' work — roles, rules, expectations — picked up from your families. Friction comes from clashing inherited scripts.
intimate.whatHappens: Each of you imported first principles from your upbringing and never examined them. The conflict isn't really about the dishes; it's about two unexamined axioms colliding.
applicationSteps: Surface the assumption: 'what do I believe a relationship 'should' do here, and where did I learn it?'
Have each partner trace a 'should' back to its origin family.
Ask together: 'what do WE actually want to build, from first principles, rather than inherit?'
Replace inherited rules with consciously chosen ones you both endorse.

concepts.title: Atomic Habits
concepts.tagline: You don't rise to your goals — you fall to your systems. And your systems are built from tiny, repeated votes for who you are.
keyPoints: Habits are the compound interest of self-improvement. A 1% daily change is invisible day-to-day, then suddenly transformative. The plateau before results is where most people quit.
The real lever is identity, not outcomes. 'I want to run a marathon' is an outcome goal; 'I am a runner' is an identity. Every action is a vote for the identity you want to become.
Behaviour change runs on a loop: Cue → Craving → Response → Reward. To build a habit, make it obvious, attractive, easy, and satisfying. To break one, invert each.
Environment beats willpower. Behaviour is a function of person AND environment. Redesign the environment — make good cues obvious, bad cues invisible — before relying on motivation.
Habit stacking leverages existing routines: 'After I [current habit], I will [new habit].' You borrow the neural pathway already in place instead of building from scratch.
strategicSteps: Start with identity: ask 'who is the kind of person who would achieve this?' Then take the smallest action that casts a vote for that identity.
Make the next habit absurdly small — 'two minutes' small. Consistency builds the identity; volume comes later.
Design your environment tonight: put one cue for a good habit in plain sight, hide one cue for a bad one.
Stack a new habit onto something you already do daily: 'After I pour my morning coffee, I will write one sentence.'
Track the streak visibly. A simple chain of ticks reinforces 'I am someone who does this.'

business.title: Protecting Deep Work
business.situation: Every Monday you intend to do focused work. By 10am you've been pulled into three 'quick' meetings and the morning is gone. Every week, the same.
business.whatHappens: You're relying on intention to protect your best hours, but the environment hasn't changed — so neither has the outcome. Habits need architecture, not resolve.
applicationSteps: Block 7:30–9:30am as visible 'no meetings' time, recurring, every day.
Replace the arrival cue (open Slack) with a deliberate one (make tea = deep work begins).
Use a two-minute on-ramp: open the document and write one line before email.
Tick a streak each day you protect the block — you're voting for 'I protect my focus.'

social.title: The Friend You Keep Meaning to Call
social.situation: Someone important to you hasn't heard from you in months. You think of them often, keep meaning to reach out, and haven't.
social.whatHappens: Relationship maintenance doesn't happen on intention alone. Waiting until you 'feel like it' or have 'enough to say' means it never happens.
applicationSteps: Set a recurring monthly reminder: send one genuine message to one person. Non-negotiable.
Stack it: every time you make morning coffee, send one short check-in.
Lower the bar radically — 'thinking of you' is a complete message; connection, not performance, is the goal.
Keep a short list of people you value and rotate through it to remove decision fatigue.

intimate.title: The Drift
intimate.situation: You and your partner used to talk differently. In the busyness of life, daily interaction became logistics and surface. You miss the connection.
intimate.whatHappens: Intimacy drifts one skipped conversation at a time, and returns the same way — one small deliberate act at a time, not one grand gesture.
applicationSteps: Introduce one daily ritual: 10 phone-free minutes with one non-logistical question — 'what was the best part of your day?'
Stack it onto something that already happens daily — dinner, tea, getting into bed.
Never cancel it for less than a real emergency; consistency is the message.
Once a month, do something you did early in the relationship — nostalgia reactivates who you are to each other.

concepts.title: Mental Models
concepts.tagline: You don't see reality — you see your model of it. The quality of your thinking is the quality of your models.
keyPoints: A mental model is a simplified representation of how something works. You can't think without them; the question is whether yours are accurate, diverse, and consciously chosen.

Munger's 'latticework': a single model makes everything look like a nail. Models from many disciplines let you triangulate — when several point the same way, confidence rises; when they conflict, you've found an interesting edge.

You don't need to master whole fields — just the 5% of each that carries 95% of the value: the foundational Big Ideas (compounding, natural selection, incentives, probability, the dichotomy of control).
Inversion is one of the most underused models: instead of 'how do I achieve X?', ask 'what would guarantee I fail at X?' then avoid those things.
Every model is wrong somewhere — it simplifies by definition. Mistaking the model for reality is the source of most intellectual error; the most useful models become invisibly 'just how things are.'
strategicSteps: Pick one field outside your expertise and learn its single most important model; apply it to a current problem.
When stuck, run the problem through multiple lenses: 'what would a biologist / economist / philosopher say?'
Practise inversion weekly: define failure explicitly, then design to avoid it.
Keep a short list of the 10 models you use most — check whether they're diverse or all from one domain.
When confident, ask 'which model am I using, and where does it break down?'

business.title: The One-Tool Decision
business.situation: Your team analyses every problem through the same single lens — always a financial model, or always a marketing frame. Different problems get the same treatment, and some keep going wrong.
business.whatHappens: The 'man with a hammer' syndrome: one model makes every problem look like the kind it solves. Important dimensions get missed because no one is looking through the right lens.
applicationSteps: Before deciding, force the problem through 3 different disciplinary lenses.
Ask 'what model am I defaulting to, and what is it blind to?'
Invite someone with a different background specifically to disagree.
Run inversion: 'what would guarantee this decision fails?'

social.title: Reading a Situation You Keep Misjudging
social.situation: You keep misreading certain social situations — assuming people are motivated by what would motivate you, and being surprised when they aren't.
social.whatHappens: You're applying a single model of human motivation (your own) to everyone. A richer latticework — incentives, status, fear, belonging — would predict behaviour far better.
applicationSteps: Ask 'what incentives is this person actually facing?' rather than 'what would I do?'
Add models: status, in-group belonging, loss aversion — run the situation through each.
Hold your first read as a hypothesis, not a conclusion.
Check predictions against what actually happens, and update the model.

intimate.title: Assuming Your Partner Thinks Like You
intimate.situation: You assume your partner processes emotion, conflict, or love the way you do — and feel hurt or confused when they clearly don't.
intimate.whatHappens: You're running a single model (yourself) for a different person. Without a model of how THEY work — their attachment style, their language of care — you keep mispredicting them.
applicationSteps: Build an explicit model of your partner: how do THEY recharge, show care, handle conflict?
Ask directly rather than assuming: 'what does feeling loved actually look like for you?'
Notice where your model of them keeps being wrong, and revise it.
Hold the difference as information, not as them being 'wrong.'

concepts.title: Emotional Regulation
concepts.tagline: You can't always choose what you feel — but you can shape how you relate to it, and that changes everything downstream.
keyPoints: Emotional regulation is the set of processes by which we influence which emotions we have, when, and how we experience and express them. It's a skill, not a personality trait.
The most effective strategy is reappraisal — changing how you interpret a situation before the emotion peaks — which beats suppression, which is costly and leaks out anyway.
Naming an emotion reduces its intensity ('affect labelling'): putting a feeling into words engages the prefrontal cortex and dampens the amygdala.
There's a gap between stimulus and response, and regulation lives in that gap. Widening it — through a pause, a breath, a name — is where freedom is.
Suppression doesn't make emotion disappear; it pushes it underground where it drives behaviour you don't consciously choose.
strategicSteps: Name it to tame it: when a strong feeling arises, label it precisely ('this is anxiety,' 'this is hurt').
Reappraise before reacting: 'what's another accurate way to see this situation?'
Build a pause habit: one breath between trigger and response widens the gap where choice lives.
Regulate the body first — emotion is physical; slow breathing and movement change the state faster than thinking does.
Don't suppress — express or process. Journalling or talking discharges what bottling only buries.

business.title: The Email That Makes You See Red
business.situation: A curt, unfair email lands. Your heart rate spikes and your fingers are already drafting a scorching reply.
business.whatHappens: System 1 emotion is driving toward a response you'll regret. Without regulation, the amygdala wins and you escalate a conflict that could have been defused.
applicationSteps: Name the feeling: 'I'm angry and a bit disrespected' — labelling lowers the intensity.
Impose a delay rule: no replies to charged emails for 60 minutes.
Reappraise: 'what's the most charitable read of why they wrote this?'
Draft the hot reply, don't send it, then write the one you'd be proud of.

social.title: Feeling Slighted in the Moment
social.situation: Someone says something at a gathering that stings. You feel the urge to snap back or go cold for the rest of the evening.
social.whatHappens: The emotion arrives faster than thought. Unregulated, it controls your behaviour and can damage a relationship over a momentary feeling.
applicationSteps: Take one slow breath before responding — it physically resets the surge.
Name internally what you're feeling to create distance from it.
Reappraise: 'did they likely mean it the way I took it?'
Choose your response from the widened gap, not the reflex.

intimate.title: Flooding During a Conflict
intimate.situation: An argument with your partner escalates until you're 'flooded' — heart pounding, unable to think clearly, saying things you'll regret.
intimate.whatHappens: Physiological flooding hijacks regulation; the thinking brain goes offline. Continuing to 'talk it out' while flooded only deepens the damage.
applicationSteps: Recognise flooding as physical and call a timeout — agree the signal in advance.
Self-soothe for at least 20 minutes (the body needs that long to settle) before returning.
Name your state to your partner: 'I'm flooded, I need a short break, I'm not leaving the conversation.'
Return when regulated — reappraise the issue once your thinking brain is back online.

concepts.title: Framing Effect
concepts.tagline: Change how something is said and you change what people decide — even when the facts are identical.
keyPoints: The same information presented differently produces different decisions. '90% survival' and '10% mortality' describe the identical outcome — but people choose very differently.
Loss frames usually hit harder than gain frames because of loss aversion: 'avoid a $50 loss' motivates more than 'save $50,' though the outcome is the same.
No communication is frame-neutral. Every sentence emphasises some aspects and backgrounds others. The only choice is whether you frame consciously or unconsciously.
Framing operates on everyone — doctors, judges, analysts — regardless of intelligence. Awareness reduces but doesn't eliminate it.
Reframing is a superpower in reverse: stripping a situation back to its underlying facts (a first-principles move) reveals the frame someone has placed on it.
strategicSteps: Before accepting any claim, ask 'what frame is this — gain or loss?' and 'what would the same fact look like in the opposite frame?'
In feedback, frame as addition not deficit: 'developing X would take you from good to excellent' beats 'you lack X.'
Know your audience's default: lead with loss framing for the risk-averse, gain framing for the growth-oriented.
Always name the cost of inaction, not just the benefit of action — 'doing nothing also costs you Y.'
When stuck or anxious, deliberately reframe: 'what is the most accurate and most useful way to describe this situation?'

business.title: The Proposal That Won't Land
business.situation: You're pitching a project as 'here's what we could gain.' Decision-makers nod politely and don't move. The upside isn't compelling them.
business.whatHappens: Risk-averse executives are moved more by avoiding loss than capturing gain. A pure gain frame leaves the cost of inaction invisible — so the safe-feeling default is to do nothing.
applicationSteps: Add the loss frame: 'without this, we risk losing Y' alongside the upside.
Match the frame to the audience — lead with risk for the cautious, opportunity for the ambitious.
In negotiation, always name the cost of NOT agreeing, changing their reference point.
Present the same numbers both ways so the decision rests on substance, not packaging.

social.title: Declining Without Damage
social.situation: You want to turn down an invitation without hurting the relationship. 'I don't want to come' is honest but lands as rejection.
social.whatHappens: The frame you choose determines whether they hear rejection or care. Same decision, very different reception depending on what you emphasise.
applicationSteps: Frame around the relationship, not your preference: 'I'd love to, but I'm depleted and wouldn't be good company.'
Emphasise what they'd lose with a depleted you, not what you're avoiding.
Offer an alternative to keep the connection ('can we do next week instead?').
Keep it specific and warm — vague excuses read as brush-offs.

intimate.title: Raising a Concern
intimate.situation: You want to tell your partner something bothers you. 'You never listen to me' frames it as a global, permanent character flaw — and triggers defence.
intimate.whatHappens: A global loss frame ('you never...') reads as a verdict and invites counterattack. A specific, behaviour-focused frame reads as a solvable issue and keeps the door open.
applicationSteps: Reframe to specific behaviour: 'when you check your phone while I'm talking, I feel unheard.'
Frame it as changeable, not as who they are — behaviour, not character.
Use a 'toward' frame to set direction ('I want us closer') and an 'away' frame for urgency ('I'm feeling distant') deliberately.
Lead with your feeling, not their fault — it's more accurate and less triggering.

concepts.title: Cognitive Dissonance
concepts.tagline: When your actions and your beliefs collide, it's usually the belief that bends — not the behaviour.
keyPoints: Cognitive dissonance is the mental discomfort of holding two contradictory beliefs, or acting against what you believe. The mind resolves it fast — usually by changing the belief, not the behaviour.
We don't reason our way to comfort; we rationalise. After a hard choice, we inflate the chosen option and disparage the rejected one to quiet the discomfort.
It explains why people defend bad decisions harder over time, why effort makes us love things (we justify the cost), and why disconfirming evidence often strengthens belief instead of weakening it.
The discomfort is the signal. Noticing the urge to rationalise — that flicker of defensiveness — is the doorway to actually learning something.

Festinger's classic study: people paid $1 to lie about a boring task later rated it more enjoyable than those paid $20 — the well-paid had an external justification, the underpaid had to change their belief.
strategicSteps: When you feel defensive, pause: 'Am I reasoning, or rationalising to reduce discomfort?'
Separate the decision from your ego — 'a past version of me chose this; present me can choose differently' removes the pressure to defend.
Write the strongest case against a decision you've already made; notice how much your mind resists.
Welcome the discomfort of being wrong as the price of being accurate — name it: 'this is dissonance, not danger.'
Delay self-justification: after a mistake, describe what happened factually before explaining why it wasn't your fault.

business.title: Defending the Failing Strategy
business.situation: You championed a strategy six months ago. Evidence now suggests it isn't working — but you find yourself arguing for it harder than ever, dismissing the data.
business.whatHappens: Admitting the strategy is wrong means admitting you were wrong — painful dissonance. So the mind protects the ego by attacking the evidence instead of updating the belief.
applicationSteps: Separate the idea from your identity: 'evaluating this strategy is not a verdict on me.'
Invite the disconfirming data explicitly and thank whoever brings it.
Ask 'if a colleague had launched this, what would I now advise them?'
Reframe changing course as competence, not failure — updating on evidence is the skill.

social.title: The Favour That Changed Your Feelings
social.situation: You did someone a big favour you didn't really want to do. Oddly, afterwards you found yourself liking them more, not resenting them.
social.whatHappens: The Ben Franklin effect via dissonance: 'I went out of my way for them' clashes with 'I don't really like them,' so the mind resolves it by deciding you must like them. Effort manufactures affection.
applicationSteps: Notice that effort creates attachment — useful to know in both directions.
If you want to build a bond, let someone do you a small favour; it engages the same effect.
Check whether your liking is genuine or a post-hoc justification for effort spent.
Don't mistake sunk effort for real compatibility.

intimate.title: Justifying What You Tolerate
intimate.situation: You stay in a situation that quietly troubles you, and you notice yourself constructing increasingly elaborate explanations for why it's fine.
intimate.whatHappens: Staying despite doubt creates dissonance, so the mind generates reasons to make the staying feel consistent. The rationalisations grow to match the gap.
applicationSteps: Notice the volume of justification — heavy rationalising signals unresolved dissonance.
Ask 'what would I tell a friend describing this exact situation to me?'
Name the discomfort directly instead of explaining it away.
Let the dissonance inform you rather than be silenced — it's data about a real gap.

concepts.title: Flow State
concepts.tagline: The fully-absorbed state where action and awareness merge, time distorts, and the work becomes its own reward.
keyPoints: Flow is complete absorption in an activity — self-consciousness fades, time warps, and performance peaks. Csikszentmihalyi found it's where people report being happiest and most fulfilled.
It appears in the channel between anxiety and boredom: the challenge must slightly exceed your current skill. Too hard breeds anxiety; too easy breeds boredom.
It requires clear goals, immediate feedback, and deep uninterrupted concentration — conditions modern life actively erodes with notifications and fragmentation.
Flow is autotelic: the activity becomes intrinsically rewarding, done for its own sake, not for an external payoff.
It's a major source of meaning and engagement — a life rich in flow tends to be a life that feels worth living, independent of pleasure or status.
strategicSteps: Match challenge to skill: tune the task slightly above your current ability to enter the channel.
Protect uninterrupted blocks — flow needs ~15+ minutes of unbroken focus to begin and dies instantly on interruption.
Set a clear goal for the session so attention has a target.
Remove friction and notifications before starting; flow can't survive a buzzing phone.
Build feedback loops so you can see progress in real time and stay engaged.

business.title: The Fragmented Workday
business.situation: You're busy all day but never feel you did anything real — pulled between messages, meetings, and tasks, never sinking into deep work.
business.whatHappens: Constant interruption makes flow impossible. You operate in shallow attention all day, which feels draining and unproductive despite the activity.
applicationSteps: Carve one protected 90-minute deep-work block with notifications off.
Pick a single clear goal for that block before you start.
Match the task difficulty to stretch you slightly — not overwhelm, not bore.
Guard the block ruthlessly; flow is destroyed by a single interruption.

social.title: Hobbies That Recharge vs Drain
social.situation: Your free time goes to passive scrolling that leaves you flat, while activities that once absorbed you sit untouched.
social.whatHappens: Passive consumption never produces flow — there's no challenge-skill match, no clear goal. The most restorative leisure is active and absorbing, not passive.
applicationSteps: Choose active, skill-engaging hobbies over passive consumption.
Pick activities slightly beyond your current ability to trigger flow.
Schedule uninterrupted time for them, as you would for work.
Notice which activities make time disappear — do more of those.

intimate.title: Shared Flow as Connection
intimate.situation: You and your partner mostly co-exist in parallel (both on phones) rather than sharing genuinely engaging experiences together.
intimate.whatHappens: Parallel passive activity doesn't build connection. Shared flow — a challenging activity you do together — creates some of the strongest bonding experiences.
applicationSteps: Find an activity you both find absorbing and slightly challenging (dancing, cooking, a sport, a project).
Do it without phones, with full attention.
Pick things that give immediate shared feedback so you're engaged together.
Notice that shared flow creates closeness no passive evening can.

concepts.title: The Planning Fallacy
concepts.tagline: We chronically underestimate how long things take — even when we've been wrong the exact same way before.
keyPoints: We systematically underestimate the time, costs, and risks of future actions while overestimating their benefits — and experience barely cures it.
The core error is taking the 'inside view': planning from the specific, optimistic details of THIS case, ignoring how similar cases actually went.
It persists because we imagine the smooth path, not the interruptions, dependencies, and setbacks that always arrive.
The fix is the 'outside view': base estimates on the actual track record of comparable projects (base rates), not on your optimistic scenario.
It compounds with optimism bias and the sunk cost fallacy — over-promising leads to over-committing leads to escalation.
strategicSteps: Take the outside view: 'how long did similar things actually take?' — then trust that over your gut.
Multiply your honest estimate by a realistic fudge factor drawn from past misses.
Break work into small pieces and estimate each — large wholes hide the slippage.
Plan for interruptions explicitly; assume the smooth path won't happen.
Track estimate-vs-actual over time to calibrate future planning.

business.title: The Deadline Everyone Misses
business.situation: Your team commits to a delivery date based on how the work would go if everything went smoothly. It never does, and you slip — again.
business.whatHappens: The inside view plans from best-case specifics and ignores the base rate of how these projects actually unfold. Optimism becomes a missed deadline and a credibility cost.
applicationSteps: Anchor estimates on the actual history of similar projects, not the ideal path.
Add explicit buffer for the interruptions that always come.
Decompose the work and estimate the parts separately.
Communicate ranges, not false-precision single dates.

social.title: Overcommitting Your Time
social.situation: You say yes to plans, favours, and projects assuming you'll have time — then find yourself overwhelmed and cancelling.
social.whatHappens: You estimate future free time from an optimistic blank-calendar fantasy, ignoring how full your weeks reliably get. The planning fallacy applied to your own life.
applicationSteps: Before committing, look at how the last few comparable weeks actually went.
Assume your future self will be as busy as your past self has been.
Build in margin; say yes to fewer things with real capacity.
Check new commitments against your real track record, not your hopes.

intimate.title: The Underestimated Effort of 'Quick' Promises
intimate.situation: You promise your partner you'll 'quickly' handle something — and it balloons, leaving them disappointed and you defensive.
intimate.whatHappens: The planning fallacy makes 'quick' promises that reality doesn't honour. Repeated small misses erode trust more than one honest larger estimate would.
applicationSteps: Give realistic estimates, not optimistic ones, even if they sound less impressive.
Under-promise and over-deliver to build trust instead of eroding it.
Factor in your real history with similar tasks before committing.
When you'll be late, communicate early rather than defending the original estimate.
